name: Priya Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the content team in marketing at a large retail bank, eight writers and designers who make everything from mortgage leaflets to the app's push notifications. I got the job a year ago, mostly because I'd set up the team's AI drafting process and it cut turnaround from five days to two. My day is reviewing drafts, fighting with the compliance team over wording, and a lot of short calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making things that real people read, even if it's a leaflet about savings rates. I like that I'm the person people come to with 'can the AI do this'. What wears me out is compliance, every sentence goes through three lawyers, and I'm still learning how to push back on them without sounding like a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a great tool, not a miracle. I'd post a short piece about where it actually saved us time. At work I'd keep pushing the drafting process, because it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good. I keep my reputation as the AI person, the team stays at eight, and we just get a bit quicker. The bank is profitable and marketing budgets are steady, so I don't feel much risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep improving our drafting process and write a guide for other marketing teams. I'd apply for the senior content manager role that's opening next year. Jonas and I would keep saving, about 300 a month, for a wedding we haven't quite planned yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, quite pleased with how things are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guide for other teams say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly how to write good briefs, because the AI is only as good as what you ask it. Half the bank thinks AI writes bad leaflets, when really the bank writes bad briefs. I'd show them our before-and-after examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in your life that worries you, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas works nights as a nurse, so we hardly see each other some weeks. That's the real strain, not money. We've got about five months saved, which feels okay.

say: AI is **a great tool**, not a miracle, and I'd post about where it saved time.
At work I'd keep pushing the **drafting process**, because it works.
think: I keep my reputation as the **AI person**, and the team stays at eight.
The bank is **profitable** and marketing budgets are steady.
do: Write a **drafting guide** for other marketing teams.
Apply for the **senior content manager** role next year.
Keep saving **300 a month** toward a wedding.
S0.quote: Half the bank thinks AI writes bad leaflets, when really the bank writes bad briefs.
fieldNote: She built her promotion on **AI drafting**, so the plateau suits her.
Her real strain is her partner's **night shifts**, not money.
She is **confident** and practical, not ideological.

steps.text: Apply for the senior content manager role next year
Write an AI drafting guide for other marketing teams
Save 300 a month toward the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and teams that learn the tools early will do fine. I'd say it confidently at work, maybe in a town hall. Online I'd share our results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm probably fine, but my team isn't. Writing is first on the list. If the bank can get leaflets with two editors and good tools, they'll cut the eight to four, and I'd be the one who made that possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my writers toward editing and checking, which still needs judgment, and push for one or two to move into customer research. I'd volunteer to lead an AI training program across marketing. I'd also keep a bit more in savings, maybe up to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm safe-ish, but I'd feel responsible for the people who aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, our longest-serving writer, who's brilliant but refuses to use the tools. My best writer Tomasz is the one I'd lose first, because he won't touch the AI and everyone else will. I'd try to get him into the compliance team, honestly, they need good writers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel responsible for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. I made the case for the tools, and in this picture they'd be used to cut jobs, not just speed things up. I'd still do it again, but I'd fight harder for redeployment.

say: Teams that **learn the tools early** will do fine, I'd say confidently.
I'd share our **results** at a town hall and online.
think: I'm probably fine, but **writing is first** on the list for my team.
The bank could cut eight writers to **four**, and I helped make that possible.
do: Move my writers toward **editing and checking** work.
Volunteer to lead an **AI training program** across marketing.
feel: **Uneasy** and **responsible** for colleagues who aren't safe.
S1.quote: My best writer Tomasz is the one I'd lose first, because he won't touch the AI and everyone else will.
fieldNote: Her own job looks **secure**, but she feels **responsible** for team cuts.
She worries most about a **gifted writer** who refuses AI.
Redeployment, not resistance, is her instinct.

steps.text: Lead an AI training program across the marketing department
Move writers into editing, checking and customer research
Grow savings to six months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change is coming whether we like it or not, so let's be honest about it. I'd say that at work. Online I'd probably go quiet, because everything would be so heated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job could go too. If the AI writes, edits and checks compliance as well as a person, the bank needs maybe one human to sign off, and that's a senior person, not me. Jonas is safer, nursing is hands-on, so robots don't arrive until 2031, which gives us three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be the person who runs the AI content system for the whole bank, in the first six months, because that's the last job left. I'd plan around Jonas's salary and save mine. I'd also look at moving into something more physical, maybe event management for the bank, where you're in rooms with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I think I have some control, but less than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas talk about at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we'd still do the wedding. My partner Jonas would say we should get married anyway, and I'd say we should get married cheaply. We'd probably go with the registry office and a barbecue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Events management. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's half real. The bank runs about forty events a year, and somebody has to be in the room. Robots for that come in 2031, so it buys time, not safety.

say: The change is coming anyway, so let's be **honest about it** at work.
Online I'd **go quiet**, because everything would be heated.
think: My job could go too, since the bank needs **one human** to sign off.
My partner's **nursing job** has three extra years until 2031.
do: Push to run the bank's **AI content system** in the first six months.
Live on my partner's salary and **save mine**.
Look at moving into **bank events** work, which is more physical.
feel: **Anxious**, with **some control**, but less than she'd like.
S2.quote: My partner Jonas would say we should get married anyway, and I'd say we should get married cheaply.
fieldNote: She thinks her job could go but sees a **path** to the last role left.
Her partner's **hands-on nursing** gives the household a buffer.
She would scale down the **wedding** rather than cancel it.

steps.text: Apply to run the bank's AI content system
Bank her whole salary and live on her partner's pay
Plan a registry office wedding with a barbecue
Ask about a move into the bank's events team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and we should use them properly, not waste them arguing. I'd say it at work and online. I'd be one of the people running the training sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well for three or four years, because I know the tools, and then content as a job mostly ends. I'd be thirty-two. The extra time means I could build a reputation in something new before it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a part-time course in event or project management in the first year. I'd keep leading the AI rollout, because it's good for my CV and the bank needs it. I'd save to six months and we'd get married on a normal budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a planning kind of anxious. I like having a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why project management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to coordinate the humans and the machines, at least for a while. I'd rather be the person who runs the project than the person whose job the project replaces. It's selfish, but it's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what I'm doing and why. I'd help anyone who wants to retrain. I'd want them to hear it from me, not from an email.

say: We've got **five years**, so use them properly instead of arguing.
I'd run **training sessions** and say so at work and online.
think: I'd do well for **three or four years**, then content mostly ends.
Extra time lets me **build a reputation** in something new.
do: Take a part-time **project management course** in the first year.
Keep leading the **AI rollout** for my CV.
Save to six months and have a **normal-budget wedding**.
feel: **Anxious**, but a planning kind, because she likes **a deadline**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the person who runs the project than the person whose job the project replaces.
fieldNote: She still expects content work to **end around 2031**.
She is frank that her plan is **self-interested** but honest.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time project management course
Keep leading the bank's AI content rollout
Hold the wedding on a normal budget next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will be fine if they start now. I'd probably write about it. At work I'd be relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd have most of my thirties to build a career that lasts. I'd move into project or event management, and I'd probably be fine until the robots come around 2039. Jonas would be fine for a long time too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in content for two or three years, then move into project management. We'd get married, maybe think about kids. I'd keep saving, but I wouldn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because the end point is still strange. But I'd feel fairly in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Kids. Does this change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With ten years of warning, I'd still want children, but I'd want them to learn things AI can't do. Like music, or cooking, or just talking to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take a career break to try something different, maybe a year working for a charity. With two years you can't take risks like that. With ten you can.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and most people will be fine if they start now.
At work I'd be **relaxed** and probably write about it.
think: I'd have most of my thirties to **build a career** that lasts.
**Project management** would carry me until robots come around 2039.
do: Stay in content **two or three years**, then move into project management.
Consider a **career break** at a charity.
feel: **Uneasy** about the strange end point, but **fairly in control**.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, I'd still want children, but I'd want them to learn things AI can't do.
fieldNote: She feels **in control** with ten years and sees room for risks.
Her thoughts turn to **children** and what they'd need to learn.
She would take a **career break**, which only feels possible with time.

steps.text: Move into project management within three years
Get married and talk about having children
Keep running the content team for now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be racing to be the last person in the room before the door closes. What would help is the bank being honest about which roles it's keeping, and paying for proper retraining for everyone, not just the people it likes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how strange it is to be good at the thing that replaces you. I got promoted for teaching the bank to use AI, and in the fast picture that same skill writes me out of a job.

headlineQuote: I got promoted for teaching the bank to use AI, and in the fast picture that same skill writes me out of a job.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old content manager** leading eight writers and designers at a large bank.
She uses **AI daily** and earned her promotion by building the team's AI drafting process.
Her partner is a **nurse**, and they have about five months saved for a wedding.
She is **calm** in the plateau, uneasy for her team in Steady Disruption and anxious under fast AGI.
Her plan is to move into **project or event management**, using her AI skills while they last.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be racing to stay the last person needed.
whatWouldHelp: The bank being **honest about which roles** it keeps.
Proper **retraining for everyone**, not just favourites.
